brief: NISA's October derivatives overview reports U.S. equity financing term structure inverted at month-end as the front end priced the higher cost of financing long positions over year-end, while the back end fell to two-year medians for the first time since May; fixed-income financing stayed near its own medians. Year-end financing spreads fell below the prior two years' levels as pressure from the June squeeze eased: asset-manager S&P 500 futures positioning fell 8.6% from its May high and levered equity ETF AUM fell 25% from its June peak, though heavy year-end IPO issuance could still weigh on dealer balance sheets and financing appetite. Equity volatility diverged on a tech-led selloff: the S&P 500 fell nearly 1% versus the Nasdaq-100's 6.65% drop (NDX -3.5% on Oct 30 alone), pushing the NDX-SPX volatility spread to near 10 points on NDX's greater AI-theme sensitivity. Treasury yields retraced September's rise and the swaption skew shifted toward receivers, signaling demand for protection against lower yields concentrated in near-term tails tied to Fed policy, not a long-term rates reassessment. Separately, the note explains persistent negative CSI 500/300/1000 financing spreads: regulatory limits on A-share short selling and access block arbitrage from closing the basis created by market-neutral hedge funds' one-way futures selling.
